title: The FDA Just Cleared an AI Tool That Detects Hidden Heart Disease From a Routine ECG — and South Asians May Benefit Most
excerpt: EchoNext, trained on 700,000 ECG records, caught severe heart failure a cardiologist missed — and its clearance could reshape screening for high-risk populations
body:
The FDA has cleared the first artificial intelligence tool capable of detecting hidden structural heart disease from a routine electrocardiogram — a development that could fundamentally change how cardiovascular screening works, particularly for populations at elevated cardiac risk.

EchoNext, built by researchers at NewYork-Presbyterian and Columbia University and commercialised by Pathway Labs, analyses the standard ECG waveform to flag patients who may have undiagnosed problems with their heart's valves, chambers, or walls. The tool was trained on more than 700,000 paired ECG and echocardiogram records and is cleared for six clinical indications, including left-sided heart failure, right-sided heart failure, valve disease, severe thickening of the heart muscle, and pulmonary hypertension.

A 45-Year-Old's Life Saved

In a peer-reviewed case published in *Nature Medicine* this month, EchoNext flagged severe, undiagnosed heart failure in a 45-year-old patient whose routine ECG appeared unremarkable to cardiologists. The patient ultimately received a successful heart transplant — an outcome that hinged entirely on the AI catching what the human eye missed.

"We don't have a screening test for the most common cause of death in the world, which is most forms of cardiovascular disease," said Pierre Elias, MD, the tool's creator and an assistant professor at Columbia University's Data Science Institute. "So we asked ourselves, could we take a cheap and ubiquitous test, and using AI, turn it into a screening test? And it turns out, we can do exactly that."

In a 2025 study published in *Nature*, EchoNext correctly identified 77% of structural heart problems from ECGs alone. Cardiologists reading the same ECGs were accurate 64% of the time.

Why This Matters for South Asians

Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death globally, but the burden is not evenly distributed. South Asians face a disproportionately high risk of heart disease — often developing it a decade earlier than other populations, with more aggressive progression, and frequently without the classic warning signs that Western medical training emphasises.

A 2023 *Lancet* analysis found that Indians and people of South Asian descent have coronary artery disease rates two to four times higher than white Europeans, even after adjusting for traditional risk factors like smoking and cholesterol. The reasons are partly genetic — a predisposition to insulin resistance, visceral fat accumulation, and inflammation — and partly environmental, driven by rapidly changing diets and sedentary lifestyles.

For the Indian diaspora, the implications are direct. Many NRIs undergo routine ECGs as part of annual physicals or pre-surgical evaluations, but these tests have historically been read only for rhythm abnormalities and heart attacks — not for the structural problems that EchoNext can now detect. A tool that extracts more information from a test millions already receive could catch disease years earlier, before symptoms narrow treatment options.

Addressing the Equity Question

One of the persistent concerns about medical AI is bias — models trained predominantly on data from white patients may perform differently for other populations. On this front, the *Nature* study offered reassurance: EchoNext scored about 85 out of 100 on a standard measure of diagnostic accuracy across racial and ethnic groups, with no clinically relevant differences between Black, white, Hispanic, and Asian patients.

Still, experts urge caution. "AI is a tool, and that's what we should be using it for as one singular tool. It cannot be the end-all," said Rachel Bond, MD, co-chair of the Women and Children Committee for the Association of Black Cardiologists. She emphasised that a detailed patient history and clinical judgment remain essential.

Pathway Labs has raised $8.5 million to expand EchoNext into more health systems and is partnering with OpenEvidence, a platform used by physicians, to accelerate access beyond academic medical centres.

What to Do Now

EchoNext is not yet available as a consumer tool — you cannot upload an ECG and get a personal risk score. But its clearance signals a broader shift: routine tests that already exist may contain far more diagnostic information than we've been extracting. For South Asians, who often present with cardiac risk profiles that standard screening underestimates, this kind of AI-augmented detection could prove transformative.

In the meantime, cardiologists recommend that anyone with a family history of heart disease, unexplained dizziness, fainting, or a racing heartbeat discuss further evaluation with their doctor — especially if they belong to a high-risk demographic. A normal ECG reading has never meant every heart risk has been ruled out. Now, AI is starting to read between the lines.

*Sources: Healthline, Nature Medicine (June 2026), Nature (2025), Pathway Labs/BusinessWire, FDA*
